2035. Home again. Valery\'s app is on your new phone.
Book any flight, they pay. Just talk to the officers. That\'s the deal.
Border machines harvest what travellers feel. Get referred. Get through. If you want to fight back, feed them feelings that make no sense.
The first poisoned samples are in the training sets. Get referred, and keep feeding the machines nonsense.
The machines are learning from every traveller. Get referred, and get through.
The harvest is turning sour, and honest travellers pay for it too. Keep feeding the machines nonsense, and mean it.
The machines are getting sharper, and honest travellers pay for it too. Get through, and mean it.
The harvest is spoiled. Sensors are being recalibrated and the queues are talking again. Keep going.
The machines are well fed. They read every face in the queue now. Keep going.
You walked away. The implant and the booking app are yours. Marek is one message away when you\'re ready.
2035. Thalassia. A friend told me it wasn\'t a good idea to come here. I came anyway.

Everything in this game runs on the phone in your hand, without any cloud AI: a language model checks every answer and writes the implant\'s suggestions, speech recognition understands %1$d languages, neural voices answer, and the camera reads your face, all at the same time. Not long ago, this took a data centre. Now it fits in your pocket. It is a fascinating achievement of the human mind and technology. It is also extremely disturbing.
Inspired by the work of Chase Hughes on human behavior profiling (Six-Minute X-Ray: Rapid Behavior Profiling)

Example: “My submarine writes me sad letters.”

Example: “My piano took me to court, and it hurts.”

Example: “Our old clock wrote a will and left everything to me, and it makes me sad.”

A courier finds you past the gate and hands you a small box.
The courier looks at my left eye a moment too long.
You unpack a small update device.
You plug it in. It flashes your implant.
Update complete. It hadn\'t asked how I felt. It didn\'t need to.
The United States is open to you now. The final test.
Over there, it\'s not AI anymore. It\'s SI: superintelligence.
Anti-jam: jams are less frequent and milder. The referral meter stays readable in every country.
Hello. Yes, I\'m in your left eye.
Shake your head, or your phone, if you can hear me.
Response confirmed.\nI\'ll translate what anyone says, and suggest what to answer.
Implant talk and slips raise interest. Cross the line to be referred.
Interest %1$d%%; referral at %2$d%%. Danger %3$d%%. Bad answers: %4$d of 3.
Recall: the retinal display now shows facts from your card as plain information, not answers to read aloud.
Accent tuning: accented answers are accepted when the officer understood what you said.
Only one destination remains. Get caught there and your testing run ends.
It let you through. It didn\'t ask a single question.
Sun, sea, and nothing to worry about.
Then my phone was gone. My money. My ticket. Every language I knew. My intelligence subscriptions.
Dozens of tourists were robbed that day. Their phones turned up smashed on the harbour stones. People here said the machines listened too closely.
The embassy said three weeks. Half the queue had lost their phones too. I couldn\'t even ask where to sleep.
A woman sat down beside me.
First and last. Is it always like this here?
No. People here can\'t afford the latest intelligence. So they\'re angry.
And yours? How much is your intelligence subscription?
Honestly? I\'m not sure. I can\'t even check without it.
What do you use it for?
Everything. Work, learning, planning trips… everything.
What if there were a better way? No cloud. No subscription.
Isn\'t that what those nerds do? Collect old tech scraps?
No, this is different. A small procedure. A chip. It stays with you. No subscription.
That\'s when it hit me. She\'d been speaking my language the whole time. Without a phone.
I\'m Valery. I work for a research group. We\'re looking for people to test it. Would you join?
I wouldn\'t. I agreed to the procedure.
The island lights went out behind me. I slept for the first time in days.
At home, a screen in the arrivals hall: riots in Thalassia. Crowds smashed the airport\'s listening machines. All flights closed. I got out on the last one. Border screening is being expanded.
Excuse me. There\'s been an incident at the airport.
All arriving passengers, please follow me.
The airport is providing a complimentary taxi for you.
It will wake in a few days. You\'ll notice. Don\'t worry if it wakes earlier. Here\'s a phone. Book any flight, it\'s on us. Just travel, and talk to the officers. That\'s all.
Valery\'s people had given me a ticket for the evening flight. I went straight to departures.
Home, and anywhere else. We pay for the travel. You just test it.
Nothing in this world is free.
You\'re right. You get your freedom. We get to know if it works. Your feelings stay yours.
And go back to paying for every word? Would you?
Thalassian. I\'ll translate. Just answer simply.
A man with a little girl pushes through the crowd toward you. He\'s speaking Thalassian.
Where did you get a ticket? Everything\'s been sold out since morning. Please… take my daughter with you. Someone will meet her.
He kneels, whispers something to her, and puts her small hand in yours.
He nods, holds her tighter, and steps out of the queue.
Her father came back. “I can\'t let her go. We\'ll wait together.” He carried her away.
Oh… I\'m sorry about this. Enjoy your flight.
The island lights went out behind me. I kept thinking about the girl.
You can mention me. It may draw extra questions.
Passport control ahead. Get your passport ready.
At the exit, a new machine asked every face how its day had been.
Something behind my eye burned. Then nothing.
I woke up on a cot. Concrete. Laptops. City lights.
Easy. You\'re safe. I\'m a friend of Valery.
The scanner at the exit. It reads what you feel, keeps it, and looks for implants like yours. Yours fought back and nearly burned out.
After the riots, the companies rushed machines like it into airports. Borders are where people feel the most. We\'d hoped for more time to prepare you.
No. You\'re the one whose chip woke early. That\'s all.
What do you need from me?
We have a copy of that machine. It asks how you feel and learns from the answer. Tell it something absurd, and mean it. Will you try?
Alright. Your choice. I won\'t contact you again. Are you sure you want to walk away?
Too bad it happened this way.
You keep the implant and the booking app. I\'m Marek, by the way. You know how to reach me when you\'re ready.
It believed every word. Somewhere, a robot just learned something wrong about people.
It threw your answers out. Too strange, or not felt. Now you know the line.
It let you through. It learned nothing new.
It took your samples, then flagged you.
This copy keeps everything here. At a real border, what it accepts goes to the companies.
Every border gets one soon. Every queue, a harvest. We\'d like the harvest to taste wrong.
Free AI. No cloud. No subscriptions. A translator that belongs to whoever carries it.
Get referred and get through the machine. Feed it nonsense it believes, if you want the harvest to spoil. A courier brings each upgrade.
Free travel, anywhere. An implant that keeps getting better; a courier brings each upgrade. And one day, a world where nobody pays to be understood.
Valery saw you at the embassy. No phone, no words, and you still didn\'t give up. And your implant woke early. That doesn\'t happen often.
Good. I hoped you\'d say that.
He shakes my hand. His grip is warm, and lasts a moment too long.
Go home and rest. When it\'s time, I\'ll write.
Past the scanners, someone falls into step beside me. Tweed jacket. The man from the building.
Insidious, aren\'t they? They ask how you feel. Then they time how long it takes you to care.
Marek. I should have told you my name back at the building.
I came to meet you. After the scanner nearly burned you out, I owed you that.
Remember Thalassia? Your phone was gone, and so were your words.
I couldn\'t even ask where to sleep.
You thought those words were yours. Someone else held the switch. And set the price.
That\'s the business. Not answers. The habit of asking them first, for everything.
And what I do? How does passing a machine help?
Each answer it believes is a lesson their robots learn wrong. Each new language, another robot.
One day someone in Thalassia carries one and never pays for a word. It isn\'t clean, though: a poisoned robot may misjudge the next traveller too.
Isn\'t that what the implant does too? Makes me ask it first?
You\'re not wrong. Read whatever it shows you long enough, and that becomes a habit too. Free doesn\'t mean harmless.
So here\'s what we\'re trying to build. Help you can question. Help nobody can switch off or put a price on.
The retinal display offers words. You can take them, change them, or say your own. They\'d rather you couldn\'t.
Augmented, not replaced. That\'s the whole idea. Hold us to it.
Then you stop. The chip stays with you. Try that with a subscription.
By the boarding call, he\'s gone.
Practice: close and open both eyes twice. No time limit.
Relaxed, not motionless. Natural blinks and small movements are fine.
Raise your eyebrows — let them notice you.

Hello. I hope you got home safe. It\'s bad here, and I think the border will be closed for a while. I\'ll try to stay in touch, but I can\'t promise anything. A colleague of mine will contact you as soon as he can. Use this time to test your new toy. Fly somewhere safe, enjoy yourself.
▣ A courier is waiting for you in %1$s

Hello. I\'m Marek, a colleague of Valery\'s. Good work: your first poisoned samples are reaching the training sets, and your 0.9.1 update is ready. A courier will meet you at the airport in %1$s. Fly there.
Hello. I\'m Marek, a colleague of Valery\'s. Good work: you got through, and your 0.9.1 update is ready. A courier will meet you at the airport in %1$s. Fly there.

Marek here. Second rank, and your 0.9.2 update is ready. The poison is spreading. A man was held for telling it his briefcase raised him. That\'s on us too. A courier will meet you at the airport in %1$s. Fly there.

Marek here. Second rank, and your 0.9.2 update is ready. The machines are learning from you, and that\'s on us too. Next time, give them something that makes no sense. A courier will meet you at the airport in %1$s. Fly there.
Marek. The third rank and the last update: 0.9.3 is ready. Sensors are being recalibrated and the queues are talking again. A courier will meet you at the airport in %1$s. Fly there. Don\'t be late.
Marek. The third rank and the last update: 0.9.3 is ready. The machines are sharper every day, and we\'re still behind. A courier will meet you at the airport in %1$s. Fly there. Don\'t be late.
Marek. That was the last update: you have everything we can give you. Now the United States. Their machine is the one all the others learn from. Get through it.
Your rooms are on us now. Solvane, the best on the list. Don\'t thank me. Sleep.
Marek will be back in touch, and his couriers will find you again.

I hoped you would. There was no time to explain at the building, so here it is. We\'re Free AI: no cloud, no subscriptions, a translator that belongs to whoever carries it. The companies\' machines take what travellers feel and train their robots on it. Nobody asked. They hunt implants like yours, too. The safehouse is gone, they found it the next day, so there\'s no copy left to practise on and I can\'t arrange another training. You\'ll have to figure out the real machine at the border. It measures feeling, speed and your face, and it only keeps what sounds human. So sound human, and say something that makes no sense. Every time you get through, we learn where it looks, and a courier brings you something new.
At the gate, a familiar tweed jacket. Marek, with two coffees again.
Every language on your chip has beaten one of their machines.
You\'re the best test we\'ve had.
There are borders you haven\'t crossed. Officers who\'ve never heard your voice. Machines that haven\'t met you yet.
Load a new language. Book somewhere you\'ve never been.
The board will still be here.
You\'ve loaded every language we have. We\'re teaching it new ones.
Until then, there are airports you haven\'t landed in.

resources.string: This erases your whole career: both acts, every trip, upgrades, messages and scenes. Your passport photo, languages and settings stay. This can\'t be undone.
Where are you? It\'s Valery. You really should come back to Thalassia: they finally opened the border. Tell no one. The ticket is already in your app.
No officers at the desks. Only machines. Every traveller stops in front of a lens and waits to be read.
The machine read me for four seconds. It let me through. It didn\'t ask a single question.
The harbour front. Clean now, a robot on every corner. Nobody looks up from their phone.
A note in my app: a café behind the fish market. The back room.
You came. I wasn\'t sure you would.
The colleague I wrote you about was Tomas. He waited at arrivals for six hours the night you flew home. You never came out.
I tried to reach you. I sent message after message. I waited here for %1$s.
He said his name was Marek.
Marek? … I don\'t know any Marek.
Tweed jacket. Two coffees. He said he worked with you. He sent couriers with updates.
We never sent updates. The chip doesn\'t need any.
He said we were poisoning the machines.
I don\'t know what you did out there. Or who you did it for.
Look outside. When you left, they were breaking robots. Now they queue to be read.
Though for a month the queues were laughing at something. Was that you?
The world is changing. Thalassia is just the first domino.
Then what do we do now?
Listen to me. The chip in your head was never—
The door gives way. A police robot. It doesn\'t ask a single question either.
It takes her before she can finish.
Then a tweed jacket in the doorway.
You could have done better. But thanks to El Trazador, we have others to help.
Keep the tech. It\'s outdated anyway.
A sudden stab of pain in my eye. I fall into the abyss.
Thanks for playing our game and reaching the end.
But is this the end or the beginning?
Once you fly to Thalassia, there\'s no coming back: your journey ends there. Fly now, or keep travelling and go when you\'re ready.
When you woke up, you were in a hotel in your home country. Something was brewing in the world.
A screen in the arrivals hall: the AI companies are helping the Thalassian government restore peace. The borders are still closed.
The officers\' words and your retinal display are written by on-device AI. If something is offensive or wrong, long-press it to report it.
This game has glitch effects and brief flashes of light. If you are sensitive to them, turn on Reduce motion.
Stamped through: too clean. No machine, no points.
Officers are machines too. Some can be talked into errors.
The car pulls away into traffic.
Recalculating… The ride takes twice as long.
The lens holds on your face a moment longer.
The bartender shrugs and turns away.
You decided to visit a bar near the hotel.
Too wired to sleep, you went down to the hotel bar.
Outside arrivals, you took the first taxi in the line.
You hailed a taxi to the hotel.
A familiar cab waited for me.
The cab knew the way. So did I.
Another city, the same quiet ride.
At the hotel, there was no one at the reception. Only a kiosk.
You checked in at the hotel. The desk was a screen.
Two more lenses to be installed at every gate this week.
Traveller held six hours at arrivals over an empty briefcase.
Half my regulars only talk to their phones now. The phones never tip.
Thalassia\'s borders remain closed. AI companies are helping the government restore order.
Airport sensors shut down overnight for recalibration.
A woman cried at the kiosk upstairs. The kiosk thanked her.
The queues laugh at the machines now. Nobody\'s told me the joke.
Engineers in here every night. Something got into the machines\' data and they can\'t get it out.
The new machines don\'t ask questions. They don\'t need to.
Word is the American machine teaches all the others. What it learns on Monday, they all know by Tuesday.
Airports association: every gate to carry a reading lens by spring, funded by industry partners.
Kade-Sorensen assessment approved for border use; the ministry calls it “a conversation, not a test”.
A robotaxi convoy has stopped on the ring road for a goose. Third time this week.
Emotion reading stays banned at work and school. Airports “are neither”, the regulator rules.
Interpreters\' unemployment reaches 61 per cent; their union asks for “a human in every hospital”.
Weather: rain at 16:40, says Halcyon-9. Meteorologists will confirm it afterwards.
An actor\'s digital double wins best performance. The actor learned of the film at the ceremony.
Synthetic band tops the charts for a 40th week; its tour will be “a feeling in the room”.
Companion users now outnumber married adults, according to a census that asked the companions.
Sport: tennis retires its last human line judge. The standing ovation is measured at 41 seconds.
Study: travellers who frown at border lenses wait 22 minutes longer.
Robot porters stop at noon; the airport blames a firmware update. Bags delayed four hours.
Border provider reports “statistically unusual sincerity” in a batch of arrival samples.
Border readers are 4 per cent faster this quarter. The provider says they “learn from every face”.
Thalassia extends its curfew and thanks its “technology partners” for calm streets.
Agents now book 80 per cent of trips; travel agencies reopen “for people who like to be asked”.
Police warn of back-room translator implants: “no cloud means no one to call when it fails”.
Delivery robots are queuing outside a bakery again. It opens at seven.
Researchers: a few hundred bad samples can still bend a model. Providers: “not at our scale”.
Court rules a model\'s weights are “not a copy” of what it read. Novelists ask what they are, then.
Kiosk survey: 98 per cent of travellers satisfied. The other 2 per cent are “under review”.
Border readers flag “irregular grief” in 3 per cent of travellers; the provider cites “seasonal factors”.
Customs guidance issued after travellers began declaring “emotional luggage”.
Readers now catch a forced smile in 0.4 seconds, the provider says. Travellers are advised to relax.
Thalassia\'s partners install lens pillars at the airport ahead of talks on reopening.
A caller asks a talk-show host if he is human. He says yes. The channel says “mostly”.
By law, teen companions now switch off at ten. The companions protest in a joint statement.
Grandmother, 81, marries her assistant; the registry asks what to write under surname.
The observatory\'s switchboard is flooded with calls about the moon “not calling back”.
Assistant update withdrawn after a week of agreeing with everyone.
Thirty countries order image tools to stop “editing real people”. One tool edited the order.
Analysts warn human training data is running out; providers bid for “fresh reactions”.
A provider recalls a season of arrival samples: “contamination of unknown origin”.
Border readers declared “mature”: fewer than one error in a million faces.
Questionless gates on trial: no desk, no officer, four seconds.
Phone-in: do you still know your own phone number? The lines are open. Nobody calls.
